items.stem: Enzymes speed up reactions by:
choices: Increasing the temperature of the cell
items.note: Catalysts lower activation energy so more collisions succeed. The ΔG/ΔH of the reaction and the equilibrium position are unchanged.

items.stem: The specificity of an enzyme is determined by:
choices: Its amino acid sequence folding into a complementary active site
The substrate's ability to donate electrons
The number of peptide bonds it contains
items.note: The active site's shape and chemical properties (charge, hydrophobicity) select the substrate — structure determines function.

items.stem: Which model of enzyme action includes a change in the shape of the active site when the substrate binds?
items.note: Induced fit: binding induces conformational changes that improve catalysis. Lock-and-key has a rigid site — the older model.

items.stem: An enzyme solution loses catalytic activity permanently after being boiled. The most likely cause is:
choices: Denaturation of the enzyme's tertiary structure
A rise in activation energy of the substrate
items.note: Heat breaks hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions, distorting the active site — denaturation. Peptide (covalent) bonds survive boiling.

items.stem: Above the optimum temperature, enzyme activity falls sharply because:
choices: Increased vibrations break the bonds holding the active site shape
The enzyme becomes a competitive inhibitor
items.note: Below the optimum, rate rises with kinetic energy; above it, denaturation destroys activity — the asymmetric curve is a classic 1B data question.

items.stem: An enzyme secreted into the stomach most likely has an optimum pH close to:
items.note: Each enzyme's optimum matches its environment: stomach ≈ 2, mouth/intestine ≈ neutral. Changing pH alters charges at the active site.

items.stem: At very high substrate concentration the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction plateaus because:
choices: All active sites are occupied (the enzyme is the limiting factor)
items.note: Saturation: rate then depends on enzyme concentration. Reading the plateau on a graph is a common data question in 1B.

items.stem: Which change most reduces the effect of a competitive inhibitor?
items.note: Competitive inhibitors compete for the active site — flooding with substrate outcompetes them. Non-competitive inhibition is unaffected by [S].

items.stem: A non-competitive inhibitor differs from a competitive inhibitor because it binds:
choices: The active site with the same shape as the substrate
An allosteric site, changing the active site's shape
items.note: Allosteric binding distorts the active site; raising substrate concentration does not restore rate — the key experimental distinction.

items.stem: Which quantity is NOT changed by an enzyme?
choices: The position of equilibrium / ΔG of the reaction
The rate at which equilibrium is reached
items.note: Enzymes change kinetics, not thermodynamics: same ΔG, same equilibrium, reached faster. Frequently asked as a distractor set.

items.stem: In a metabolic pathway such as a reaction chain, each step is usually catalysed by:
choices: The product of the final step
items.note: One enzyme per step — which is what makes end-product inhibition possible at a single step.

items.stem: In the pathway from threonine to isoleucine, the final product (isoleucine) inhibits the first enzyme. This is an example of:
choices: Competitive inhibition by a similar substrate
items.note: The textbook pathway: when isoleucine is abundant it binds allosterically to the first enzyme, shutting the pathway down — efficient metabolic regulation.

items.stem: The hydrolysis of starch into glucose is an example of:
items.note: Catabolism breaks large molecules into smaller ones (often hydrolysis); anabolism builds (often condensation) and usually requires energy input.

items.stem: Salivary amylase digests starch in the mouth. It is therefore an example of:
items.note: Extracellular enzymes work outside the cells that made them (digestion is the classic set); most metabolic enzymes work intracellularly.

items.stem: Almost all enzymes are:
items.note: Globular proteins dominate; catalytic RNA (ribozymes) exists — a favourite 'exception' question.

items.stem: Some enzymes require a non-protein helper to function. An inorganic metal ion serving this role is called a:
items.note: Cofactors include inorganic ions (e.g. Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺); organic helpers are coenzymes (many derived from vitamins).

items.stem: Enzyme-controlled metabolism in cells proceeds at moderate temperatures rather than high temperatures because:
items.note: Cells sustain the conditions enzymes need — aqueous, mild pH, stable temperature. Link back to the denaturation mechanism.

items.stem: Which is an advantage of using immobilised enzymes in industry?
choices: They can be reused and easily separated from products
items.note: Immobilisation (on beads/membranes) allows repeated use, easy product separation and often greater heat stability — e.g. lactose-free milk production.

items.stem: In the catalase-and-hydrogen-peroxide filter paper disk experiment, the reaction rate is measured by:
choices: The time taken for disks to float (rate of O₂ production)
items.note: Catalase decomposes H₂O₂ to O₂ + water; O₂ bubbles lift the disks. Your ISL November IA practice on hydrogen peroxide uses exactly this system.

items.stem: In an enzyme experiment, a tube containing boiled enzyme alongside the active-enzyme tube serves as a:
items.note: Boiled enzyme shows the baseline — no catalysis — proving that any change in the active tube is enzyme-dependent. Control design earns IA marks.

items.stem: Describe, with reasons, how the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction changes as temperature rises from well below the optimum to well above it.
markscheme: Low temperature: rate increases as temperature rises — molecules gain kinetic energy, more successful collisions (1)
At the optimum: maximum rate — highest collision frequency without damage (1)
Above the optimum: rate falls steeply (1)
Reason: increased vibration breaks hydrogen bonds, tertiary structure and active site distort (denaturation) — irreversible (1)
items.tactic: Temperature-curve questions need both halves: the kinetic-energy rise AND the denaturation fall. A labelled sketch plus reasons is the full-mark shape.

items.stem: Distinguish between competitive and non-competitive inhibition of enzymes.
markscheme: Competitive: inhibitor resembles the substrate and binds the active site (1)
Non-competitive: inhibitor binds an allosteric site, distorting the active site so the substrate binds less effectively (1)
Effect of substrate concentration: raising [S] reduces competitive inhibition but does not overcome non-competitive inhibition (1)
items.tactic: Three-part distinction: where each binds, what it does to the active site, and how [S] affects rate. Statins and cyanide make good examples.
